quote: Für welche Werte von $\lambda$ ist durch die beiden Bedingungen $y=0$ für $x=a$ und für $x=b$ die Lösung $y=0$ nicht die einzige.
english: For which values of $\lambda$ is the solution $y=0$ not the only one under the two conditions $y=0$ for $x=a$ and for $x=b$?
topic: Notes on conformally mapping a surface in R4 onto a ring in the plane via a cyclide, an iterative linearization method for second-degree (quadratic) ordinary and partial differential equations, a proof idea for the independence of the distributive law from the other arithmetic axioms, and the eigenvalue problem for y'' + λA(x)y = 0 with boundary conditions.

triage.modern_statement: This is the classical Dirichlet Sturm–Liouville eigenvalue problem. Find all λ for which y'' + λA(x)y = 0 on [a,b], with y(a) = y(b) = 0, has a solution other than y ≡ 0. These λ are the eigenvalues. Typical questions are whether eigenvalues exist, whether they are real, discrete and infinite in number, how they grow, and how often the eigenfunctions oscillate. If A(x) > 0, this is the standard 'definite' case. If A changes sign (the 'indefinite' or 'non-definite' weight case), Hilbert's school called it 'polar'.
triage.answered_by: Sturm and Liouville answered the positive-weight case in their 1836–37 papers. Hilbert and his Göttingen school (Hilb, Haupt) used integral equations to handle the case where A changes sign, which they called 'polar'. R.G.D. Richardson, who went to Göttingen in 1908, published oscillation and eigenvalue results for that case in 1912–1918, including Math. Ann. 73 and Amer. J. Math. 40 (1918), pp. 283–316. Later spectral theory with indefinite weights was done in Krein spaces by Everitt, Daho–Langer and others.

evidence.claim: In 1836–1837 Sturm and Liouville published a series of papers that started Sturm–Liouville theory. It covers equations of the form (p y')' + q y = λ w y.
Sturm–Liouville theory gave the first theorems on eigenvalue problems and on the properties of eigenvalues.

A survey of the non-definite Dirichlet Sturm–Liouville problem says Hilbert and his school called such problems 'polar'. It discusses Richardson's results, Hilb's special case and Haupt's treatment, and notes that Richardson went to Göttingen in 1908.

Richardson's 1918 paper (Amer. J. Math. 40, pp. 283–316) studied oscillation properties of Sturm–Liouville problems with an indefinite weight. Later work treats these problems in a Krein space generated by the weight.
Indefinite Sturm–Liouville operators are still studied today, for example in 'polar form'.

triage.why: The note says exactly what the Dirichlet eigenvalue problem for y'' + λA(x)y = 0 is. It is not an open research question. Sturm and Liouville already answered it in 1836–37 for positive A. Hilbert's own integral-equation work (1904–1912) and his students and visitors (Hilb, Haupt, Richardson) worked out the sign-changing 'polar' case. It is not one of Hilbert's 23 problems or the 24th problem. The basic question is settled. Spectral theory with indefinite weights, especially singular problems in Krein spaces, is still an active field. The sources do not show whether the note was written before or after Sturm–Liouville theory was standard, or whether Hilbert meant positive or sign-changing A. That is why the note is marked 'unclear'.
